derivations.claim: In one dimension set $y=\sqrt{\beta/(2m)}\,x$; the substitution and [F1] give $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\beta x^2/(2m)}dx=\sqrt{2\pi m/\beta}$. Taking the product of $d$ such factors and applying [F2] repeatedly gives the displayed exact $d$-dimensional integral.

Put $\alpha=\beta_0/(2m)>0$. For any integer $s\ge1$, the function $x\mapsto |x|^{2s}e^{-\alpha x^2/2}$ is bounded: it is continuous on $[-1,1]$ and tends to zero at both infinite ends. Hence $|x|^{2s}e^{-\alpha x^2}\le C_{s,\alpha}e^{-\alpha x^2/2}$; on $[-1,1]$ the same bound holds after increasing $C_{s,\alpha}$. By the scaled one-dimensional Gaussian integral, both $\int e^{-\alpha x^2}dx$ and $\int |x|^{2s}e^{-\alpha x^2}dx$ are finite.

For $\beta\ge\beta_0$, $e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m)}\le e^{-\alpha|p|^2}$. If $s\ge1$, $(\sum_{i=1}^d p_i^2)^s\le d^{s-1}\sum_{i=1}^d|p_i|^{2s}$; for $s=0$ the weight is one. A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its boundary $\partial E$ is null, equivalently has content zero.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, and suppose $Dg(x)$ is invertible for every $x\in U$. Let $K\subseteq U$ be compact and Jordan measurable. For a bounded function $f:g(K)\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is Riemann integrable on $g(K)$;
2. $x\mapsto f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|$ is Riemann integrable on $K$.

When either condition holds,
$$\int_{g(K)}f(y)\,dy=\int_K f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|\,dx.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: Fix a sphere of radius $r>0$. At least one coordinate of every point on it has absolute value at least $r/\sqrt3$. On each of the six patches where a specified coordinate is largest in absolute value and has a specified sign, write that coordinate as $\pm\sqrt{r^2-u^2-v^2}$ over a bounded disk with $r^2-u^2-v^2\ge r^2/3$. The graph gradient is uniformly bounded. A grid of squares of side $\delta$ covers the disk with $O(\delta^{-2})$ squares; the graph over each square fits in a rectangular box of base area $\delta^2$ and height $O(\delta)$, so the total covering volume is $O(\delta)$. Thus the sphere has content zero. The sphere at radius zero is a point and is covered by one cube of arbitrarily small volume. Since $\partial A_{a,b}$ is contained in the union of the spheres of radii $a$ and $b$, [F1] makes the bounded shell Jordan measurable.

If $a=b$, then $A_{a,b}$ is a sphere of Jordan content zero by step 1.1, so both integrals are zero. Now assume $0<a<b$. For $0<\varepsilon<\min\{\pi/4,(b-a)/2\}$ put $K_\varepsilon=[a,b]\times[\varepsilon,\pi-\varepsilon]\times[\varepsilon,2\pi-\varepsilon]$ and $\Psi(r,\theta,\phi)=(r\sin\theta\cos\phi,r\sin\theta\sin\phi,r\cos\theta)$. On the open domain with $r>0$, $0<\theta<\pi$ and $0<\phi<2\pi$, $\Psi$ is injective and $C^1$ with determinant $r^2\sin\theta>0$; its inverse is given by radius, polar angle and the unique azimuth in $(0,2\pi)$. The compact set $K_\varepsilon$ is Jordan, and [F2] makes $x\mapsto F(|x|)$ integrable on $\Psi(K_\varepsilon)$. Applying [F3] gives
$$\int_{\Psi(K_\varepsilon)}F(|x|)\,dx=\left(\int_a^bF(r)r^2\,dr\right)\left(\int_\varepsilon^{\pi-\varepsilon}\sin\theta\,d\theta\right)(2\pi-2\varepsilon).$$

The missing part of $A_{a,b}$ outside $\Psi(K_\varepsilon)$ is contained in the union of the polar-cap box $[-b\sin\varepsilon,b\sin\varepsilon]^2\times[-b,b]$ and the azimuth-seam box $[-b,b]\times[-b\sin\varepsilon,b\sin\varepsilon]\times[-b,b]$. Their total volumes are at most $8b^3(\varepsilon^2+\varepsilon)$, which tends to zero. Since $F$ is bounded, the difference between its integral on the whole shell and on $\Psi(K_\varepsilon)$ tends to zero. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ in step 2.1 gives the formula and the angular factor $2\cdot2\pi=4\pi$. If $a=0$, first apply the result to $[\eta,b]$ and then let $\eta\downarrow0$; the omitted ball lies in $[-\eta,\eta]^3$ and contributes at most $8\eta^3\sup_{[0,b]}|F|$, while the absolute value of the omitted radial integral is at most $\sup_{[0,b]}|F|\eta^3/3$. Both tend to zero.

Use SI dimensions for the numerical model parameters: Newton constant $G$ has units $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, each mass $m_i$ has units $\mathrm{kg}$, each position $q_i$ has units $\mathrm{m}$, each momentum $p_i$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, energy $H$ has units $\mathrm{J}$, Boltzmann constant $k_B$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, and inverse energy $\beta$ has units $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. Fix an action reference $h_*>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$; it is a normalization convention and is not identified with Planck's constant.

For an integer $N\ge1$, any Lebesgue measurable position region $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and equal particle mass $m>0$, define the ordered phase space $\Gamma_N=B^N\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with coordinates $(q_1,\ldots,q_N,p_1,\ldots,p_N)$. This phase space and measure are allowed even when $B$ is unbounded or has infinite volume; finite canonical preparations separately require a positive finite partition integral. The dimensionless reference measure for identical classical particles is
$$
d\nu_N=\frac{d^{3N}q\,d^{3N}p}{N!h_*^{3N}}.
$$
For a measurable real Hamiltonian $H$ and $\beta>0$ with $0<Z_N(\beta):=\int_{\Gamma_N}e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu_N<\infty$, define the canonical density $p_\beta=Z_N(\beta)^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ relative to $\nu_N$. For a probability density $\rho$ with $\int|\rho\log\rho|\,d\nu_N<\infty$, define its reference-relative entropy $S(\rho)=-k_B\int\rho\log\rho\,d\nu_N$.

When $H$ is fixed and a Gibbs-volume function $\Omega(E)=\nu_N\{H\le E\}$ satisfies $0<\Omega(E)<\infty$, the Gibbs-volume entropy convention is $S_G(E)=k_B\log\Omega(E)$ and its temperature is defined by $1/T_G=dS_G/dE$ where that derivative exists and is positive. If $\omega(E)=\Omega'(E)>0$, a distinct surface-entropy convention with fixed energy width $\Delta E>0$ is $S_B(E)=k_B\log(\omega(E)\Delta E)$. These conventions are definitions; they need not assign the same finite-system temperature.

The measure is dimensionless because $d^{3N}q\,d^{3N}p$ and $h_*^{3N}$ have the same units. The definition supplies no physical assertion that the chosen Hamiltonian describes nature and no mechanism of dynamical equilibration.

Use the phase space and dimensionless reference measure of [[def-tgr-gravitating-phase-reference]]. Fix an integer $N\ge1$, a bounded Lebesgue measurable $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with positive finite volume, a common mass $m>0$, a gravitational coupling $G>0$, and a softening length $a>0$. On $\Gamma_N=B^N\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ define
$$H_{N,a}(q,p)=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{|p_i|^2}{2m}+U_a(q),\qquad U_a(q)=-\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}\frac{Gm^2}{\sqrt{|q_i-q_j|^2+a^2}}.$$
The positions and momenta are mathematical phase variables; the softening is a fixed regulator parameter. The Hamiltonian is measurable and its potential is bounded because each pair denominator is at least $a$. A point-particle model is a different Hamiltonian and is not included at $a=0$.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, $m>0$, and $0<\beta_0\le\beta_1<\infty$. For every $\beta\in[\beta_0,\beta_1]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m)}\,dp=\left(\frac{2\pi m}{\beta}\right)^{d/2}.$$
For every integer $s\ge0$, the polynomially weighted Gaussian has a uniform finite bound
$$\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_0,\beta_1]}\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+|p|^{2s})e^{-\beta|p|^2/(2m)}\,dp<\infty.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Each pair denominator is at least $a$, so $-C_N\le U_a\le0$ and $K_N\ge0$. Consequently $e^{-\beta K_N}\le e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}\le e^{\beta C_N}e^{-\beta K_N}$. Tonelli [F4] and [F2] evaluate the momentum integral as $(2\pi m/\beta)^{3N/2}$; the position integral is $|B|^N$, so the stated positive lower and finite upper bounds follow after division by $N!h_*^{3N}$.

Fix a compact interval $[\beta_0,\beta_1]\subset(0,\infty)$. Since $|U_a|\le C_N$ and $K_N=|p|^2/(2m)$ in $d=3N$ momentum coordinates, for every fixed $j$ there is a finite $A_j$ such that
$$|H_{N,a}|^j e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}\le A_j(1+|p|^{2j})e^{-\beta_0|p|^2/(2m)}$$
for every $\beta\in[\beta_0,\beta_1]$ and every phase point. The right side is integrable by [F2] times the finite position volume $|B|^N$. This proves all absolute energy moments and supplies an integrable compact-parameter envelope.

For each $j$, the parameter derivative of $(-H_{N,a})^j e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}$ is $(-H_{N,a})^{j+1}e^{-\beta H_{N,a}}$; its measurability and an integrable uniform bound are provided by step 2.1 at order $j+1$. Apply [F3] successively on compact subintervals of $(0,\infty)$, starting with $j=0$, to differentiate under the integral any finite number of times. The formula for $Z_N^{(j)}$ follows by induction, and the moment of order zero gives the positive normalized density.

$$\Omega(-e)=\frac{(4\pi)(4\pi/3)(2\mu)^{3/2}A^3}{h_*^3}e^{-3/2}J(\delta), \qquad \delta=\frac{er_0}{A}.$$
The integration interval is compact and has positive length, while the integrand is continuous and positive in its interior, so $\Omega$ is finite and strictly positive.

Since $J'(\delta)=-\delta^{1/2}(1-\delta)^{3/2}$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus, differentiating the explicit formula with $E=-e$ yields
$$\Omega'(E)=\frac{(4\pi)(4\pi/3)(2\mu)^{3/2}A^3}{h_*^3}e^{-5/2} \left[\frac32J(\delta)+\delta^{3/2}(1-\delta)^{3/2}\right]>0.$$

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$
Here $q_*=0$ by convention when $I$ is empty; for nonempty $I$ the displayed supremum is unchanged. In the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. Define the positive diagonal multiplier $G_{\beta,\mu}$ by $G_{\beta,\mu}|m\rangle=e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}|m\rangle$. Then $G_{\beta,\mu}$ is trace class, with
$$
\Xi_B=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty,\qquad \Xi_F=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1+q_j)<\infty.
$$
Thus $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}G_{\beta,\mu}$ is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. For fixed $\mu$, if for every compact $B\subset J\subset(0,\infty)$ a summable $(a_m)$ satisfies $(1+|E(m)-\mu|m||^2)e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}\le a_m$ for all $m$ and $\beta\in B$, then $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\mathbb E(K_\mu)$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(K_\mu)$. If $(\beta,\mu)$ varies over an open set and a summable compact-parameter envelope dominates $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}(1+|E(m)|^2+|m|^2)$, then at fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$. These stronger moment envelopes are additional hypotheses, not consequences of trace-class normalization.

For a finite mode set $J$, the canonical fixed-number coefficients are defined by
$$
\prod_{j\in J}(1-ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}=\sum_{N\ge0}Z_{B,N}(J)z^N,\qquad \prod_{j\in J}(1+ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})=\sum_{N=0}^{|J|}Z_{F,N}(J)z^N.
$$
Each coefficient is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over the corresponding number sector; for a countable mode set it is the increasing limit over finite mode sets and is finite under the stated grand-trace hypotheses. A fixed-number law is the grand law conditioned on total number, so its occupations are generally coupled. The oscillator specialization uses the actual one-particle Hermite basis and diagonal domain of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], not a formal differential eigenfunction list.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Use the dimensionless phase reference of [[def-tgr-gravitating-phase-reference]] and the softened Hamiltonian of [[def-tgr-softened-gravity-finite-phase]].

1. For two equal positive masses in a bounded three-dimensional box with nonempty interior, the distinct point Hamiltonian
$$H_2^{\mathrm{pt}}(q,p)=\frac{|p_1|^2+|p_2|^2}{2m}-\frac{Gm^2}{|q_1-q_2|}$$
makes the canonical partition integral infinite for every $\beta>0$.

2. For fixed $a>0$, let $B_N$ be a sequence of bounded boxes containing one fixed cube $C$ of volume $v>0$ and diameter $D<\infty$, with constants $b_1,b_2>0$ such that $b_1N\le |B_N|\le b_2N$. The softened canonical partition functions satisfy
$$\frac{\log Z_N(\beta)}{N}\ge \beta c(N-1)-\log N+K_\beta, \qquad c=\frac{Gm^2}{2\sqrt{D^2+a^2}}>0,$$
where $K_\beta$ is independent of $N$. Hence $\log Z_N/N\to+\infty$ and the free energy per particle $-\beta^{-1}\log Z_N/N$ tends to $-\infty$.

3. For the unscaled point attraction $-Gm^2/r$ restricted to the hard-core position domain $D_N=\{q\in B_n^N:|q_i-q_j|>a\text{ for }i\ne j\}$ with fixed $a>0$, there is a fixed-density sequence of integers $n\ge2$, $N=n^3$, boxes $B_n=(0,nd)^3$ of side $O(n)$ for fixed $d>a$, and positive-volume admissible position sets on which the interaction energy is at most $-c_0N^{5/3}$ for some $c_0>0$. Its canonical partition functions therefore also satisfy $\log Z_N/N\to+\infty$.

These three model-family statements rule out automatic ordinary extensive stability from finite volume or short-distance regularization alone. They do not rule out differently scaled interactions or all possible gravitational thermodynamic limits.

derivations.claim: Fix a grid spacing larger than the hard-core radius and take $N=n^3$ particles, one in each small cube around the cubic grid sites. The enclosing box has side proportional to $n=N^{1/3}$ and the product of the small cubes is an admissible positive-volume position set, matching [F1].

By [F1], the attraction on those configurations is at most $-c_0N^{5/3}$ and the Gaussian momentum integral contributes only an exponential factor of order $e^{O(N)}$; thus $\log Z_N/N\to+\infty$ and $F_N/N\to-\infty$. This contradicts the claimed extensive free-energy bound.

Under [[def-tgr-regulated-kepler-shell-law]], let $E=-e$, $\delta=er_0/A\in(0,1/16]$, and
$$z(\delta)=\frac{\delta^{3/2}(1-\delta)^{3/2}}{J(\delta)},\qquad \mathcal B(\delta)=\frac32+z(\delta).$$
For the Gibbs-volume entropy $S_G(E)=k_B\log\Omega(E)$ and temperature convention $1/T_G=dS_G/dE$,
$$T_G(E)=\frac{e}{k_B\mathcal B(\delta)},\qquad C_G(E):=\frac{dE}{dT_G} =-\frac{k_B\mathcal B(\delta)^2}{\mathcal B(\delta)-\delta\mathcal B'(\delta)}<0.$$
The denominator is at least $1$. This is a finite regulated mathematical branch with the stated entropy convention; it does not identify a universal operational temperature or dynamical stability.

Use the relative Kepler Hamiltonian and shell $Q=\{q\in\mathbb R^3:r_0\le|q|\le R\}$ from [[def-tgr-regulated-kepler-shell-law]], with $\mu,A,r_0>0$ and $R>16r_0$. For every $\beta>0$, define
$$Z_{\mathrm{rel}}(\beta)=\frac1{h_*^3}\int_Q\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-\beta h(q,p)}\,d^3p\,d^3q.$$
Then
$$0<\frac{|Q|e^{\beta A/R}}{h_*^3}\left(\frac{2\pi\mu}{\beta}\right)^{3/2} \le Z_{\mathrm{rel}}(\beta) \le \frac{|Q|e^{\beta A/r_0}}{h_*^3}\left(\frac{2\pi\mu}{\beta}\right)^{3/2}<\infty.$$
All energy moments are finite, and on every compact positive $\beta$ interval one integrable majorant justifies all derivatives of $Z_{\mathrm{rel}}$. The normalized canonical density has
$$\langle h\rangle_\beta=-\partial_\beta\log Z_{\mathrm{rel}},\qquad \frac{d\langle h\rangle_\beta}{d\beta}=-\operatorname{Var}_\beta(h),\qquad C_K:=\frac{d\langle h\rangle_\beta}{dT_K}=k_B\beta^2\operatorname{Var}_\beta(h)\ge0, \quad T_K=(k_B\beta)^{-1}.$$

Use SI dimensions for the numerical model parameters: Newton constant $G$ has units $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, each mass $m_i$ has units $\mathrm{kg}$, each position $q_i$ has units $\mathrm{m}$, each momentum $p_i$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, energy $H$ has units $\mathrm{J}$, Boltzmann constant $k_B$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, and inverse energy $\beta$ has units $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. Fix an action reference $h_*>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,s}$; it is a normalization convention and is not identified with Planck's constant.

For an integer $N\ge1$, any Lebesgue measurable position region $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and equal particle mass $m>0$, define the ordered phase space $\Gamma_N=B^N\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with coordinates $(q_1,\ldots,q_N,p_1,\ldots,p_N)$. This phase space and measure are allowed even when $B$ is unbounded or has infinite volume; finite canonical preparations separately require a positive finite partition integral. The dimensionless reference measure for identical classical particles is
$$d\nu_N=\frac{d^{3N}q\,d^{3N}p}{N!h_*^{3N}}.$$
For a measurable real Hamiltonian $H$ and $\beta>0$ with $0<Z_N(\beta):=\int_{\Gamma_N}e^{-\beta H}\,d\nu_N<\infty$, define the canonical density $p_\beta=Z_N(\beta)^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ relative to $\nu_N$. For a probability density $\rho$ with $\int|\rho\log\rho|\,d\nu_N<\infty$, define its reference-relative entropy $S(\rho)=-k_B\int\rho\log\rho\,d\nu_N$.

When $H$ is fixed and a Gibbs-volume function $\Omega(E)=\nu_N\{H\le E\}$ satisfies $0<\Omega(E)<\infty$, the Gibbs-volume entropy convention is $S_G(E)=k_B\log\Omega(E)$ and its temperature is defined by $1/T_G=dS_G/dE$ where that derivative exists and is positive. If $\omega(E)=\Omega'(E)>0$, a distinct surface-entropy convention with fixed energy width $\Delta E>0$ is $S_B(E)=k_B\log(\omega(E)\Delta E)$. These conventions are definitions; they need not assign the same finite-system temperature.

The measure is dimensionless because $d^{3N}q\,d^{3N}p$ and $h_*^{3N}$ have the same units. The definition supplies no physical assertion that the chosen Hamiltonian describes nature and no mechanism of dynamical equilibration.

Let $0\le a<b<\infty$ and let $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The closed radial shell $A_{a,b}=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:a\le|x|\le b\}$ is Jordan measurable, and
$$\int_{A_{a,b}}F(|x|)\,dx=4\pi\int_a^b F(r)r^2\,dr.$$
The angular area measure used below is the pushforward of $\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi$ on $[0,\pi]\times[0,2\pi]$ under $(\theta,\phi)\mapsto(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)$; its total mass is $4\pi$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
Fix $E=-e<0$. For the cutoff domain $r\ge\varepsilon>0$, the momentum sublevel at radius $r$ is the ball $|p|\le\sqrt{2\mu(A/r-e)}$ for $\varepsilon\le r\le A/e$. Applying [F2] to the momentum ball and the position shell and using [F4] gives
$$\Omega_\varepsilon(-e)=\frac{(4\pi)(4\pi/3)(2\mu)^{3/2}}{h_*^3} \int_\varepsilon^{A/e}r^2(A/r-e)^{3/2}\,dr.$$
As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, the sublevel sets increase to the full relative phase sublevel, so [F3] gives $\Omega(-e)=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\Omega_\varepsilon(-e)$. With $s=er/A$ this is
$$\Omega(-e)=C e^{-3/2}J_0,\qquad C=\frac{(4\pi)(4\pi/3)(2\mu)^{3/2}A^3}{h_*^3},\quad J_0=\int_0^1s^{1/2}(1-s)^{3/2}ds.$$
The integral $J_0$ is finite and positive because its integrand is bounded by $s^{1/2}$ near zero and by $(1-s)^{3/2}$ near one.
Since $E=-e$, differentiation gives $\omega(E)=\Omega'(E)=\frac32 C J_0 e^{-5/2}>0$. The Gibbs-volume entropy therefore has $T_G=2e/(3k_B)$ and $C_G=dE/dT_G=-3k_B/2$.

For any fixed $\Delta E>0$, the surface-density entropy has $\omega(E)\Delta E=(\frac32 C J_0\Delta E)e^{-5/2}$, so $T_B=2e/(5k_B)$ and $C_B=dE/dT_B=-5k_B/2$. Both temperatures are positive under their declared conventions, but $C_G\ne C_B$.

This explicit six-dimensional relative model contradicts convention-independent finite-system heat capacity. Its bound-energy phase volume is finite at each $E<0$; no canonical normalizability, finite outer box, or empirical preparation is claimed.

Let $S_1\in C^2(I_1)$ and $S_2\in C^2(I_2)$ be entropies on open energy intervals, with $S_i'(E_i)=1/T_i(E_i)>0$ and finite nonzero heat capacities $C_i=dE_i/dT_i$. At a common-temperature critical point of
$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x)=S_1(x)+S_2(E_{\mathrm{tot}}-x),$$
one has
$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}''(x)=-\frac1{T^2}\left(\frac1{C_1}+\frac1{C_2}\right).$$
In particular, if $C_1<0<C_2$, the critical point is a strict local entropy maximum in this energy-exchange direction whenever $0<C_2<|C_1|$.

This condition is realized by taking the first subsystem from the negative-capacity branch of [[thm-tgr-regulated-kepler-negative-capacity]] and a finite bath entropy
$$S_b(E_b)=C_b\log\left(\frac{E_b-E_0}{C_bT_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right)+S_0,\qquad E_b>E_0,$$
with $C_b>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, $E_0$ in $\mathrm J$, and $T_{\mathrm{ref}}>0$ in $\mathrm K$. It has $T_b=(E_b-E_0)/C_b$ and heat capacity $C_b$; choose $E_b=E_0+C_bT_*$ to match the subsystem temperature $T_*$ and choose $C_b<|C_1|$.

Separately adopt the effective scalar exchange equation
$$\dot x=L S_{\mathrm{tot}}'(x),\qquad L>0\ \mathrm{J\,K\,s^{-1}}.$$
Near any strict local maximum $x_*$ with $S_{\mathrm{tot}}''(x_*)<0$, this dynamics has a forward invariant local basin and an exponentially attracting solution, and along every solution $dS_{\mathrm{tot}}/dt=L(S_{\mathrm{tot}}')^2\ge0$. This is stability of the specified one-dimensional exchange law, not of a general relativistic star or a causal transport equation.

derivations.claim: Differentiating the displayed bath entropy gives $S_b'(E_b)=C_b/(E_b-E_0)$, so $T_b=1/S_b'(E_b)=(E_b-E_0)/C_b$ and $dE_b/dT_b=C_b$. The chosen $E_b$ makes $T_b=T_*$.

Since $C_b=|C_G|/2$, the reciprocal-capacity sum is $1/C_G+1/C_b=-1/|C_G|+2/|C_G|=1/|C_G|>0$. At the matched-temperature critical point, [F1] gives
$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}''=-\frac1{T_*^2}\left(\frac1{C_G}+\frac1{C_b}\right) =-\frac1{T_*^2|C_G|}<0.$$
Thus the combined entropy has a strict local maximum in this exchange direction.

The selected effective law $\dot x=L S_{\mathrm{tot}}'(x)$ has nonnegative entropy production and exponentially attracts this local maximum by [F1]. This is a constructed mathematical reservoir model, not empirical data or a generic gravitational stability conclusion.
